---
title: "Bayes at the Edge"
abstract: |
  Accuracy-first epistemology defends conditionalization by showing that, among rules that respond only to what one learns, it does best by the lights of accuracy. Externalists who hold that inexact knowledge needs a margin for error face a problem: such agents can learn something without learning that it is what they learned, and then other rules do better. Meehan and Zhang argue that conditionalization can be restored: among "globally evidentially constant" rules, it has the highest total expected accuracy summed over every learning situation. I argue that the restoration fails for exactly the agents who motivate it. If every way an agent has of learning about a magnitude carries a two-sided margin for error, then whatever she learns, the truth lies in its interior and never at its edge. A rule that responds only to what she learns, but discounts its edges, is then at least as accurate as conditionalization at every possibility and more accurate whenever what she learns has an edge. Conditionalization comes back only when the evaluation counts learning in which the truth sits at the edge of what is learned. That is what coarsening at random requires, and what margins forbid. The externalist must give up the accuracy explanation, margins around the truth, or conditionalization.
bibliography: bayes-at-the-edge.bib
---

# The problem {#sec-intro}

Bayesian conditionalization says that on learning *p*, and nothing stronger, one should adopt one's prior conditional on *p*. Its best-known defence is accuracy-theoretic. @GreavesWallace2006 showed that, if the propositions one might learn form a partition, then among plans that respond only to what one learns, conditionalizing has the highest expected accuracy. @BriggsPettigrew2020 turned this into a dominance argument: a prior together with a non-conditionalizing plan is accuracy-dominated by some alternative. Both results presuppose that whenever one learns *p*, one is in a position to tell that *p* is what one learned.

Externalists deny this. On @Williamson2000's view, inexact knowledge requires a margin for error. If the hand of an unmarked clock points at 17 and you cannot discriminate neighbouring positions, then the most you know by looking is that it points somewhere from 16 to 18. Had it pointed at 18 you would have known only that it pointed from 17 to 19. Since 18 is compatible with what you know, you do not know that 16 to 18 is what you know. When learning is opaque in this way, the accuracy arguments turn against conditionalization. Among plans that respond only to what is learned, the one with highest expected accuracy conditionalizes on the proposition that one has learned *p*, not on *p* itself [@Schoenfield2017]. In the clock that plan makes one certain of the hand's exact position. The externalist who wants to be a Bayesian and to keep a connection between rationality and accuracy appears to be stuck [@Schultheis2025].

@MeehanZhang2025 offer a way out. They require that the credence a rule recommends depend only on the prior and the proposition learned, not on the learning situation that produced it. They call this *global evidential constancy*. And they evaluate rules not by expected accuracy in the situation the agent is actually in, but by *total* expected accuracy: the sum of expected accuracies over every learning situation compatible with the prior. Their main result (Fact 10, p. 330) is that among globally evidentially constant rules, conditionalization uniquely maximizes total expected accuracy. Bayes is back.

I will argue that Bayes is back only for learners who lack the feature that made the problem. My central claim is a dominance result. Suppose every way an agent has of learning about a magnitude carries a two-sided margin for error, as Williamson's clock and Meehan and Zhang's own examples do. Then whatever she learns, the truth lies in its interior: never at a point next to a possibility the proposition excludes. A globally evidentially constant rule that discounts the edges of what is learned is at least as accurate as conditionalization at every possible combination of learning situation and state, and strictly more accurate whenever what is learned has an edge (@sec-dominance). Put informally: knowing that you cannot tell neighbouring cases apart is information about where, within what you know, the truth lies. Conditionalization throws that information away, and pays for it at every possibility you leave open.

How, then, does Meehan and Zhang's total come out in conditionalization's favour? Their measure is an instance of what statisticians call *coarsening at random*: for each proposition, the weight on learning it is the same at every state where it is true, including states at its edge (@sec-edge). Margins around the truth forbid exactly this. So the evaluation that brings Bayes back counts learning that the agents who motivated the problem cannot do. I consider Meehan and Zhang's best reply, that rules are to be evaluated across all learners who share a prior, in @sec-whose. I conclude that the externalist must give up one of three things: the accuracy explanation of conditionalization, margins around the truth, or conditionalization itself (@sec-conclusion).

Some of this has antecedents, which I will flag as I go. That Meehan and Zhang's total amounts to expected accuracy when every learning situation is equally likely was observed by Kenny Easwaran in a comment on a blog post of Richard Pettigrew's [@Pettigrew2025]. The likelihood-weighted rules that maximize expected accuracy under uncertainty about how one learns are in @Gallow2021, @IsaacsRussell2023 and @EaswaranNielsen2025. @Salow2018 contrasts evidence centred on the truth with evidence centred on a best guess, though for a different purpose. @Dorst2020 uses a single-proposition dominance argument against some clock models. What is new here is a dominance result that holds uniformly across every two-sided learning situation and is witnessed by a globally evidentially constant rule; the diagnosis of how every vindication of conditionalization escapes it; and the trilemma that results.

# Margins around the truth {#sec-margins}

I use Meehan and Zhang's framework. A *prior space* is a finite set of states *S* with a regular prior π. A *learning situation* is a function *E* taking each state *s* to the strongest proposition *E*(*s*) one learns there. Learning is factive, so *s* ∈ *E*(*s*). A learning situation is *transparent* if the propositions *E*(*s*) partition *S*, and *opaque* otherwise. An *updating rule* takes a prior space and a learning situation and returns, for each state, the credence to adopt there. A rule is *globally evidentially constant* if the credence it recommends at *s* depends only on (*S*, π) and *E*(*s*). Equivalently (their Fact 5, p. 316), it is a function from propositions to credences: *f*(*p*). Conditionalization, *b*(*p*) = π(· | *p*), is one such rule.

Now give the states the structure of a scale. Think of them as the positions of a clock hand, or the weights of a lump of butter in sufficiently small increments, ordered on a line or around a circle. Two states are *neighbours* if they are adjacent. The increments are fine enough that the agent cannot discriminate neighbours: as Williamson puts it for his clock, "the difference between neighbouring positions is well below your threshold of discrimination" [@Williamson2014, p. 979].

Williamson's margin-for-error principle says that if one knows *p* at *s*, then *p* is true at every state close enough to *s* that one cannot discriminate it from *s*. If what one learns is what one comes to know, which Meehan and Zhang cite as "one influential externalist view of evidence" (p. 290, n. 4), then the strongest proposition learned at *s* contains the neighbours of *s*. Call a learning situation *two-sided* if, for every state *s*, *E*(*s*) contains *s* and both of its neighbours (or its one neighbour, at the end of a line). The margins may be wider than one step, may differ from state to state, and may be asymmetric beyond the immediate neighbours. All that is required is that no state can be told apart from the states next to it.

For a proposition *p* ⊆ *S*, let its *interior* be the set of states in *p* all of whose neighbours are also in *p*, and its *rim* the rest of *p*: the states of *p* that sit next to a state *p* excludes. Then:

**Observation.** If *E* is two-sided and *E*(*s*) = *p*, then *s* is in the interior of *p*.

The proof is a line. If *s* were on the rim, one of its neighbours would lie outside *p*, but a two-sided *E*(*s*) contains all of *s*'s neighbours. Williamson proves the special case for his clock: when what is known at *w* is the interval of width 2*h*+1 centred on *w*, "R(w) is known only at w" [@Williamson2014, p. 980]. Meehan and Zhang's Olivia is another case. She "knows that, if the butter weighs *x* oz., then she will learn by weighing it in her hand that it weighs (*x* ± 1) oz., but nothing more precise" (p. 294). So she learns that the butter weighs between 16 and 18 oz. only if it weighs 17. Their Dana, who weighs butter that is 15, 16 or 17 oz. with her right hand (p. 300), learns {15, 16} only at 15. In general, whatever a two-sided learner learns, the truth is not at its edge.

The Observation applies to the models of inexact knowledge that generate the externalist's opacity: margins drawn around the truth. Some writers draw them instead around something the agent can track, such as a best guess or an appearance, and allow the truth to fall anywhere within the margin of the guess, including at its edge [@Stalnaker2009; @CohenComesana2013; @Salow2018]. On those models much of the opacity disappears; that was Salow's point in introducing them. The measurement models of @Williamson2013 and @Weatherson2013, on which the strongest thing known after a reading *a* with error *e* and margin *m* is that the value lies within *e* + *m* of *a*, belong to the first family. Since the true value lies within *e* of *a*, every value within *m* of it is still within *e* + *m* of *a*: the margin around the truth is preserved. Meehan and Zhang's opacity is margin-around-the-truth opacity. Olivia and Dana are their illustrations, and Olivia is "a variant of the austere clock from Williamson" (p. 294, n. 6).

# Conditionalization is dominated {#sec-dominance}

An accuracy measure assigns a score *A*(*c*, *s*) to a credence function *c* at a state *s*. Two standard measures will do for illustration. The logarithmic score is ln *c*(*s*). The Brier score is the negative squared Euclidean distance between *c* and the credence function that is certain of *s*. Meehan and Zhang sum squared errors over every proposition rather than every state, but on probability functions over *n* states the two differ only by the factor 2^*n*−2^.[^brier]

[^brier]: Write *d* = *c* − *v*~*s*~, where *v*~*s*~ is certain of *s*, so that Σ~*i*~ *d*~*i*~ = 0. Then Σ~*A*⊆*S*~ (Σ~*i*∈*A*~ *d*~*i*~)² = Σ~*i*,*j*~ *d*~*i*~*d*~*j*~ · #{*A* : *i*, *j* ∈ *A*} = 2^*n*−2^ Σ~*i*~ *d*~*i*~².

Define two globally evidentially constant rules. When the interior of *p* is nonempty, let *f*~log~(*p*) = π(· | int *p*), the prior conditioned on the interior; and let *f*~Br~(*p*) be the closest point to π(· | *p*), in Euclidean distance, among credence functions that give all their probability to the interior. When the interior is empty both rules simply conditionalize. A two-sided learner never learns such a proposition.

**Proposition.** Let π be regular. For every two-sided learning situation *E* and every state *s*,

* ln *f*~log~(*E*(*s*))(*s*) ≥ ln π(*s* | *E*(*s*)), and
* the Brier score of *f*~Br~(*E*(*s*)) at *s* is at least that of π(· | *E*(*s*)),

with strict inequality in both cases whenever *E*(*s*) has a nonempty rim. On a connected scale, that means whenever anything short of the whole space is learned.

*Proof.* Let *p* = *E*(*s*). By the Observation, *s* is in the interior of *p*. For the log score, π(*s* | int *p*) = π(*s*)/π(int *p*) ≥ π(*s*)/π(*p*) = π(*s* | *p*), and the inequality is strict iff π gives the rim positive probability, which regularity guarantees when the rim is nonempty. For the Brier score, let *c* = π(· | *p*) and let *q* be its projection onto the convex set *K* of credence functions concentrated on int *p*. For any point *y* of *K*, ‖*c* − *y*‖² ≥ ‖*c* − *q*‖² + ‖*q* − *y*‖², because the angle at *q* is not acute. The credence function certain of *s* is in *K*, so *q* is at least as close to it as *c* is, and strictly closer when *c* ∉ *K*, which holds iff the rim is nonempty. ∎

Four remarks.

First, both rules respond only to what is learned. They satisfy evidential constancy and non-contrastiveness, hence the idempotence that Meehan and Zhang defend at length (§4.3). Nothing in global evidential constancy rules them out. Nor does anything in followability distinguish them from conditionalization: as Meehan and Zhang themselves point out, conditionalization is no more "luminous" than its rivals in opaque problems (p. 306). A rule that tells you to conditionalize on what you learned asks no less of your capacity to tell what you learned than a rule that tells you to discount its edge.

Second, the dominating rules can be made conservative in Meehan and Zhang's sense, refusing certainty in anything one's evidence does not entail (p. 300). If the accuracy measure is concave, as both the log and Brier scores are, then for any ε between 0 and 1 the mixture (1 − ε)*f* + ε*b* scores at least (1 − ε)*A*(*f*) + ε*A*(*b*) at every state, which is strictly more than *A*(*b*) wherever *f* does strictly better. This is the technique of Meehan and Zhang's own Fact 4 (p. 304). The mixtures give every evidence-compatible state positive credence and still dominate conditionalization. On the clock with *f*~log~ and ε = 0.3 the result is credence 0.1, 0.8, 0.1 in the three positions one cannot rule out, the "concentrated" credence @AhmedSalow2019 consider, though only for the sake of argument.

Third, some numbers. Suppose Olivia's prior is uniform over 15 to 20 oz. When the butter weighs 17 she learns [16, 18]. Conditionalization gives each of the three weights credence 1/3. Both dominating rules make her certain of 17, and she is right, since [16, 18] is learned only at 17. When Dana's butter weighs 15 she learns {15, 16}, and conditionalization recommends (0.25, 0.75, 0). Its Brier score, on Meehan and Zhang's all-propositions measure, is −2.25 (p. 302). That is worse than the −2.08 of simply keeping her prior, which is their Fact 3. The dominating rule scores 0. The conservative mixture with ε = 0.2, (0.85, 0.15, 0), scores −0.09.

Fourth, the uniformity is the point. Meehan and Zhang observe that for any globally evidentially constant rule there are problems in which another such rule does better, and conclude: "There is no rule that rules them all" (p. 327). Their Fact 7 (p. 324) says that no such rule does at least as well as conditionalization in every updating problem. The proof uses, for each proposition *p*, the transparent problem in which one learns whether *p*. There *p* is learned at every state where it is true, including its rim. Restrict attention to two-sided problems and the situation is reversed: a single rule does at least as well as conditionalization in every one of them, and strictly better in all but the trivial ones.

It follows that no weighting of learning situations, however interpreted, can make conditionalization the most accurate globally evidentially constant rule if it gives weight only to two-sided situations and gives some weight to learning something nontrivial. For accuracy-first epistemology, dominance is the strongest verdict there is [@Joyce1998; @Pettigrew2016]. The proposition says that for an agent who knows that all her learning carries two-sided margins, conditionalization is dominated by an option she has.

How does this relate to existing dominance arguments? @BriggsPettigrew2020 show that, for partitional learning, any plan other than conditionalization is dominated (see @Nielsen2021 for corrections to their theorem). The present result is a mirror image for two-sided learning, where no learning is partitional. @Dorst2020 argues that natural versions of Williamson's clock produce "effacing evidence", in which the rational credence in a single proposition is dominated by a constant credence, and takes this as a reason to reject such models. That is a dominance argument about one proposition, used against margin models. The Proposition concerns the whole updating rule, holds for every two-sided situation and every regular prior, and is neutral about whether margin models are right. @Das2022 shows that conditionalizing plans in a known opaque inquiry can be exploited in betting. @Schoenfield2017's meta-conditionalization beats conditionalization in expected accuracy, but it responds to the learning situation and not only to what is learned. The dominating rules here do not.

# How Bayes comes back {#sec-edge}

Why, then, does Meehan and Zhang's total favour conditionalization? Their generalization of it is instructive. Let λ assign non-negative weights to learning situations, and let λ~*p*~(*s*) be the total weight of situations in which *p* is learned at *s*. Meehan and Zhang show (Lemma 1, p. 344) that the globally evidentially constant rule with the highest λ-weighted total expected accuracy assigns each state a credence proportional to π(*s*)λ~*p*~(*s*). If λ is read as a probability of being in each learning situation, this is just conditionalization on the fact that *p* was learned, with λ~*p*~(*s*) playing the role of a likelihood. This is the observation Easwaran made: the total is "basically equivalent to assuming you are equally likely to be using it in any of these situations" [@Easwaran2025]. And it is the likelihood-weighted rule of @Gallow2021, @IsaacsRussell2023 and @EaswaranNielsen2025. Conditionalization on *p* comes out best iff λ~*p*~(*s*) is the same at every state of *p*. That is Meehan and Zhang's condition of *extensionality* (Fact 11, p. 337; Lemma 2, p. 345).

The condition has a name in statistics. Data are *coarsened at random* when the probability of observing a set is the same at every point of the set [@HeitjanRubin1991; @Gill1997]. @GrunwaldHalpern2003 show that conditioning on the observation itself coincides with conditioning on the fact that it was observed iff the data are coarsened at random. In the words of @GillGrunwald2008 [p. 2410], the condition "precisely characterizes when one can ignore the distinction between the fact that an event has been observed, and the fact that an event has happened". The Monty Hall problem is the standard illustration, as Meehan and Zhang note in discussing Pearl's lesson that "we must also consider what information could have been reported" (p. 311, n. 21). Their extensionality is coarsening at random, and Fact 11 is an instance of the statistical characterization.

Meehan and Zhang's own measure, which weights every factive learning situation equally, satisfies it. In Easwaran's gloss, which proposition one learns is "chosen uniformly at random from the set of all propositions true at the world" [@Easwaran2025]. For globally evidentially constant rules, the total therefore credits each proposition *p* as if it were learned equally often at each of its states.[^perm] That includes the rim, where the true state sits next to one that *p* excludes.

[^perm]: More generally, any weighting that is unchanged when the states are permuted is extensional. If *s* and *s*′ are both in *p*, the transposition of *s* and *s*′ maps the situations that deliver *p* at *s* one-to-one onto those that deliver *p* at *s*′, preserving weight. The counting measure is permutation-invariant because it treats *S* as an unstructured set; a weighting that respects the order of a scale need not be.

For a two-sided learner this is not merely contestable, as Meehan and Zhang allow when they call extensionality "bedrock" (p. 337). It is impossible. By the Observation, λ~*p*~ is zero on the rim of *p* for any weighting supported on two-sided situations. So such a weighting is extensional only if every proposition with positive weight has an empty rim. On a connected scale, that means nothing nontrivial is ever learned. In the statistical idiom: margins around the truth guarantee that coarsening is not at random. This is a one-line consequence of the characterization in @GrunwaldHalpern2003 [Theorem 3.1]. Their observation that coarsening at random holds for overlapping observations only in special cases is its general background.

Coarsening at random can be restored with mixed learning situations, but only by adding learning that is exact at the edge. Suppose, on Dana's scale, we mix her right-hand situation with gauges that err in one direction only:
- one that, at 15, can tell that the weight is exactly 15;
- one that, at 16, can tell that it is not 17;

and so on, in the right proportions.[^cx] The mixture is coarsened at random and conditionalization is again optimal. The gauges that make this work are the ones with no margin on the side facing the excluded possibility: they deliver {15, 16} at 16, which a two-sided learner never does. And the proportions must be exact. The weightings that are coarsened at random form a lower-dimensional subset of the weightings on any support that includes a two-sided situation, so a weighting chosen at random from such a support almost never is.

[^cx]: With weights 2/7, 1/7, 1/7, 1/7, 2/7 on the situations that deliver, at 15, 16 and 17 respectively, ({15}, *S*, *S*), ({15, 16}, *S*, {16, 17}), (*S*, {15, 16}, {16, 17}), (*S*, *S*, {17}) and (*S*, {16, 17}, *S*), the weight on learning {15, 16} is 1/7 at both of its states, on {16, 17} it is 2/7 at both, and on *S* it is 4/7 at all three.

The same pattern runs through the models in which conditionalization has looked accuracy-friendly despite opacity. @Carr2021's clock spreads prior credence evenly over world–evidence pairs, so that each piece of evidence is equally likely at each of the three positions it leaves open. Isaacs and Russell's clock lets one's guess fall equally often one step either side of the truth. Easwaran and Nielsen's continuous dial with uniform error within the margin is conditionalization-friendly, they note, because "for every signal, every world that gives it a non-zero probability gives it the same probability" [@EaswaranNielsen2025, p. 1120]. In each case the truth is as likely to be at the edge of what is conditioned on as in its middle. That is what margins around the guess allow and margins around the truth forbid. When Easwaran and Nielsen make the error more likely near the guess (p. 1129), the optimal update is no longer conditionalization on anything.

Coarsening at random also explains a family of familiar anomalies, though only in one direction. When learning is coarsened at random, conditionalizing on what one learns is conditionalizing on a partition of a richer space. So it inherits the properties that make conditionalization attractive in the transparent case: its expected posterior equals the prior, and its expected accuracy is at least that of not updating [@Good1967]. Predictable bias and negative value of evidence under conditionalization [@Salow2018; @AhmedSalow2019; @Das2023; Meehan and Zhang's Fact 3] therefore all require that coarsening at random fail, and two-sided margins guarantee that it does. The converse fails. Williamson's symmetric clock is not coarsened at random, yet conditionalization there is unbiased and does better than the prior. Whether a particular anomaly appears depends on the prior and on the ends of the scale. The dominance result needs none of this.

# Whose accuracy? {#sec-whose}

Here is the best reply I can construct on Meehan and Zhang's behalf. Updating rules are shared by every agent with a given prior space. Total expected accuracy is meant to be "part of an objective measure of how accurate the updating rule is in general for any agent, irrespective of their uncertainties about their evidential situations" (p. 330, n. 35). The edge-discounting rule is tuned to one discriminative structure, and for agents who learn differently it is a disaster. Take Dana's left hand, which "can tell … whether or not it weighs 17 oz." (p. 320). With it she learns {15, 16} at 16, and the rule that discounts the edge then makes her certain of 15. Under the log score that is infinitely bad, and under Meehan and Zhang's equal weighting the edge-discounting rule loses to conditionalization by a wide margin.[^nums] Conditionalization is the rule that sacrifices no class of learners to another. The knowledge Dana has of her own margins is knowledge about her learning situation, not about the weight of the butter, and non-contrastiveness says it should make no difference. And the closing remarks of "Bayes Is Back" already allow that a "low-level" rationality, sensitive to "individual psychological dispositions and environmental conditions", may diverge from "high-level" Bayesian rationality (p. 338).

[^nums]: On Dana's prior space, with all-propositions Brier scores, the edge-discounting rule of @sec-dominance averages −1.58 per learning situation under Meehan and Zhang's equal weighting, against −0.68 for conditionalization; under the log score its average is −∞.

I have six responses.

*The domain of evaluation.* Dominance arguments compare options across the agent's epistemic possibilities [@Joyce1998; @Pettigrew2016]. Olivia and Dana are stipulated to know how they learn: that is what makes them opaque learners rather than learners uncertain about their own methods. Across Olivia's epistemic possibilities conditionalization is dominated. Meehan and Zhang's total ranges over learning situations she knows she is not in. So the dispute is no longer about weights, which Meehan and Zhang treat as bedrock. It is about the domain over which rules are compared. On that question accuracy-first epistemology already has a principle, and the principle favours the agent's epistemic possibilities.

*Global evidential constancy is not at issue.* The dominating rules satisfy it. Nothing in the argument relies on Dana's knowledge of her margins being part of her evidence. The edge-discounting rule responds to {15, 16} in the same way whoever learns it. Non-contrastiveness rules out responding to the learning situation one is actually in; it does not rule out responding to the shape of what one learns.

*Impartiality is a compromise.* On the population reading, conditionalization is the best single policy for a community of learners with a common prior and different ways of learning, some exact at the edge and some not. Grant that. For every member of the community whose learning is two-sided, following the policy costs accuracy at every possibility she leaves open, a sure loss and not merely an expected one. Pettigrew's summary of the result is that "the negative expected effects of being exposed to certain evidence functions and conditionalizing on them are counterbalanced by the positive expected effects of doing this when exposed to other evidence functions" [@Pettigrew2025]. The counterbalancing is done by other learners. Meehan and Zhang compare their proposal to rule consequentialism ("do not jaywalk", p. 289; n. 37). But rule consequentialists ask individuals to bear costs for the sake of a code because codes must be taught, accepted and coordinated on [@Hooker2000]. Meehan and Zhang explicitly do not rest global evidential constancy on followability (p. 308), and none of the other reasons applies to an idealized agent planning her own updates.

*Uncertain margins.* An agent may not know exactly how she will learn. If she is certain only that her learning is two-sided, with margins of unknown and varying width, the Proposition still applies, since it uses nothing more. If she gives some credence to learning that is exact at an edge, such as Dana unsure which hand she will use, dominance fails, and the question is one of expected accuracy under her credences. Then Lemma 1 applies, and conditionalization is optimal only if her credences happen to be coarsened at random, which, as we saw, is a knife-edge. In every other case some evidence-constant rule does better in expectation.

*Two levels.* Suppose Meehan and Zhang take the two-level option, so that Bayesianism is the theory of high-level rationality. Then the high level is the rationality of learners without margins around the truth. It is not the rationality of Olivia, Dana's right hand, or the clock-watcher, the cases used on p. 294 to motivate externalism. Meehan and Zhang write that "one does not have to be an internalist to subscribe to extensionality; the principle is compatible with evidence externalism as well" (p. 338). That is true of externalism in general. It is not true of the margin-based externalism their examples rely on.

*Absurdity.* The pure dominating rule makes one certain that one is not at the edge of what one knows. On Williamson's clock it makes one certain of the hand's exact position, an inference @AhmedSalow2019 [p. 6] call implausible. I agree that it is implausible. But the Proposition shows where the implausibility comes from. If margins are drawn around the truth, then what one learns carries information about where the truth lies within it, and an accuracy-first theory cannot ask an agent to discard information that would make her more accurate at every possibility. If using the information is absurd, the culprit is the model of evidence, as Salow suggests, and not the rule that uses it. The conservative versions, which merely discount the edge, are not absurd. They match the natural thought that when you can just rule out 15 and 19 oz., 17 is a better bet than 16 or 18. None of them is conditionalization.

# Conclusion: a trilemma {#sec-conclusion}

The externalist Bayesian wanted three things: conditionalization; opacity of the kind generated by margins around the truth; and an explanation of conditionalization's rationality in terms of accuracy. The Proposition shows that she cannot have all three.

She can keep conditionalization and margins and give up the accuracy explanation. Rational credence is then evidential probability, the prior conditioned on one's evidence, as a basic norm [@Williamson2000; @Das2022]. This is the first of the externalist responses Meehan and Zhang describe and hoped to improve on (p. 288).

She can keep accuracy and conditionalization and give up margins around the truth. Margins are then drawn around something the agent can track [@Stalnaker2009; @CohenComesana2013; @Salow2018]. On such models learning is much closer to transparent, and the opacity that set the problem largely disappears. Conditionalization survives because there is little left for it to survive.

Or she can keep accuracy and margins and give up conditionalization for rules that discount the edges of what is learned. These are the likelihood-weighted rules of @Gallow2021, @IsaacsRussell2023 and @EaswaranNielsen2025, here with a likelihood fixed by the structure of inexact knowledge itself.

Meehan and Zhang's theorem is correct, and it shows something real: averaged over every way of learning, the selection effects that hurt conditionalization cancel. But they cancel because the average includes learners who can learn a proposition at its edge. For learners whose knowledge always has a margin around the truth, nothing cancels. Bayes is back only where the truth can sit at the edge of what one knows.
